followups.q: What design smell can inheritance reveal?
followups.a: A subclass that disables or violates inherited behavior may not be a true subtype.

followups.q: Does composition always eliminate coupling?
followups.a: No. It moves coupling to collaborator contracts and can add unnecessary delegation if overused.

questions.trap: Using inheritance only to reuse implementation when the subtype cannot honor the base contract.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; no company claims. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 7.5 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron)).

questions.question: What does the Liskov substitution principle require from a subtype?
questions.answer: A subtype should be usable wherever its base type is expected without breaking the base contract. In practical terms, an override should not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions or violate invariants clients rely on. Java's compiler checks signature and exception compatibility, but it cannot prove behavioral substitutability. A classic warning is a subtype that throws UnsupportedOperationException for a base operation callers reasonably expect to work. I test implementations through the abstraction and design interfaces around capabilities that implementations can genuinely provide. When behavior cannot be substituted, separate interfaces or composition may model the relationship more honestly.

followups.q: Can Java compilation guarantee Liskov compliance?
followups.a: No. It enforces type rules, not the full behavioral contract.

followups.q: What is a symptom of a weak base abstraction?
followups.a: Subclasses routinely reject inherited operations or require callers to know concrete types.

questions.trap: Equating successful compilation with behavioral substitutability.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; general design principle, not an attributed company pattern.

questions.question: Why can passing null to an overloaded constructor be ambiguous?
questions.answer: The null literal can be converted to any reference type, so if overloads accept unrelated reference types, the compiler may have no most-specific applicable constructor. If one parameter type is a subtype of another, overload resolution may select the more specific one instead. Primitive parameters cannot accept null without boxing to a reference type. I avoid ambiguous overload sets, use named static factories when construction meanings differ, or cast null explicitly only when the intended overload is genuinely clear. This is compile-time overload selection; no runtime object's class exists for a null argument to resolve the call.

followups.q: Can runtime dispatch resolve an ambiguous null overload?
followups.a: No. Overload resolution happens at compile time, and an ambiguous call does not compile.

followups.q: What API can avoid constructor overload ambiguity?
followups.a: Named static factories can express distinct construction intent without relying on argument type inference.

questions.trap: Assuming a null argument is resolved using the runtime class of the intended object.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; overload resolution edge cases should be checked by compilation.

questions.question: What do instanceof and casts do when the reference is null?
questions.answer: The instanceof operator returns false when its left operand is null, so it can be used as a null-safe type test. Casting a null reference to a compatible reference type succeeds and still produces null; dereferencing it later causes NullPointerException. A cast checks runtime compatibility when the reference is non-null and throws ClassCastException if the object is not an instance of the target type. Pattern matching for instanceof combines the test and binding but preserves the same null non-match behavior. I use these rules to separate absence handling from type compatibility and avoid casts that mask an unclear object model.

followups.q: Does casting null to String throw ClassCastException?
followups.a: No. The cast succeeds and the resulting reference is null.

followups.q: Does null instanceof String return true?
followups.a: No. It evaluates to false.

questions.trap: Confusing a successful null cast with a non-null object of the target type.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; standard Java reference-cast behavior.

questions.question: When can a reference cast fail at runtime, and how should unchecked casts be contained?
questions.answer: A checked reference cast tests whether a non-null object is compatible with the target runtime class and throws ClassCastException otherwise. A generic cast can be unchecked when erasure prevents the runtime from validating type arguments, so it may appear to succeed and fail later when an element is read. I avoid raw types and isolate any necessary unchecked conversion in one small, documented helper with a clear invariant. At external boundaries, I validate actual element types instead of trusting a generic signature supplied by unsafe code. Suppressing a compiler warning does not add runtime validation.

followups.q: Can a cast to List<String> verify every element?
followups.a: No. Generic arguments are erased, so elements may fail later when read as String.

followups.q: Does SuppressWarnings make an unchecked cast safe?
followups.a: No. It hides a diagnostic but does not establish the required invariant.

questions.trap: Treating an unchecked cast as runtime validation of generic element types.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; no company claims.

questions.question: Why must a subclass exception catch appear before its superclass catch?
questions.answer: A catch block for a superclass handles instances of its subclasses too. If that broad catch appears first, a later catch for a specific subclass can never be reached, so the compiler rejects the unreachable handler. I order catches from the narrowest recoverable condition to broader failures, and make each branch's response intentional. When multiple unrelated types share exactly the same handling, multi-catch can reduce duplication. Catch ordering affects which recovery logic runs, not the inheritance or original type of the thrown object. I avoid broad catches that convert unrelated failures into the same misleading result.

followups.q: Can IOException be caught before FileNotFoundException?
followups.a: No; the superclass catch would make the subclass catch unreachable.

followups.q: What is a sensible catch order?
followups.a: Handle specific recoverable exception types before broader supertypes.

questions.trap: Putting catch(Exception) before more specific checked exception handlers.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; Java compiler reachability rule.

questions.question: How do regex semantics and the limit argument affect String.split?
questions.answer: String.split treats its delimiter as a regular expression, not necessarily a literal character. Characters such as a dot or pipe need escaping or Pattern.quote when intended literally. The limit controls the number of resulting pieces and how trailing empty strings are handled: a positive limit bounds splitting, zero discards trailing empty results, and a negative limit preserves them. These distinctions matter in CSV-like parsing, although split is not a complete CSV parser because quoting and escaping rules are richer. I select an explicit limit when trailing fields or remainder content are meaningful and test empty input and delimiters at boundaries.

followups.q: What does a zero split limit do to trailing empty fields?
followups.a: It discards trailing empty strings from the result.

followups.q: Is split on commas a complete CSV parser?
followups.a: No; quoted fields, escapes and embedded delimiters require a format-aware parser.

questions.trap: Using split with an unescaped regex metacharacter or losing meaningful trailing empty fields.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; regex and split-limit details should be tested for the chosen delimiter.

questions.question: When is StringJoiner useful compared with StringBuilder?
questions.answer: StringJoiner is designed for appending elements with a delimiter and optional prefix and suffix, such as a comma-separated display value or bracketed list. It avoids manual separator bookkeeping and can be combined with Collectors.joining in stream pipelines. StringBuilder is more general when assembly has varied control flow or formatting. Neither performs escaping for CSV, JSON or SQL; a delimiter join is not a serializer. I choose based on output format and use a format-aware library when fields can contain delimiters, quotes or protocol-specific escaping. Empty input behavior should be defined deliberately, especially when prefix and suffix are present.

followups.q: Does StringJoiner quote fields for CSV?
followups.a: No. It inserts delimiters and optional wrappers but does not implement CSV escaping.

followups.q: Can a stream use the same join semantics?
followups.a: Yes, Collectors.joining supports delimiter and optional prefix and suffix.

questions.trap: Using simple joining as a substitute for protocol serialization and escaping.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; output-format rules remain application-specific.

questions.question: How do length and capacity differ in StringBuilder?
questions.answer: StringBuilder length is the number of characters currently in the sequence, while capacity is the amount of storage available before the backing buffer needs to grow. Setting length can truncate or extend the logical sequence, with newly exposed positions filled according to the API; ensureCapacity requests room without adding characters. Capacity is a performance detail, not output length. I may provide an estimate when constructing a large known result to reduce growth reallocations, but avoid depending on exact growth policy. If the builder is reused, I clear or reset its logical length and ensure prior sensitive content is not retained longer than necessary.

followups.q: Does ensureCapacity change length?
followups.a: No. It may reserve storage without changing the current sequence.

followups.q: What does setLength(0) do?
followups.a: It makes the logical sequence empty, though backing storage may remain allocated.

questions.trap: Reporting capacity as the number of characters currently present.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; internal buffer growth strategy is implementation-specific.

questions.question: How can interfaces help reduce concrete collection coupling in an API?
questions.answer: Accepting or returning an interface such as List or Map lets callers depend on required operations instead of one implementation class. That makes substitution easier, but the interface still carries meaningful contracts such as ordering, mutability, null handling and concurrency. Returning an unmodifiable List does not communicate every implementation detail through the type, so documentation and tests may be needed for important guarantees. I avoid exposing a concrete ArrayList unless callers truly need its specific behavior, and I avoid choosing an overly broad Collection when indexed access or uniqueness is part of the contract. Abstraction should hide irrelevant details without hiding semantics.

followups.q: Does returning List guarantee the caller can mutate it?
followups.a: No. The interface type alone does not promise mutability.

followups.q: Why not always return Collection?
followups.a: A narrower or more specific interface can communicate required behavior such as indexing or uniqueness.

questions.trap: Assuming an interface type erases important behavioral guarantees such as order or mutability.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; API design pattern only, no company claim.

questions.question: Can you create an object of an abstract class in Java?
questions.answer: No. Calling new on an abstract class is a compile-time error, because the class may leave methods unimplemented and a complete object of exactly that type cannot exist. Two things look like exceptions but are not. A reference of the abstract type can point at a concrete subclass instance, as in Shape s = new Circle(); the object is a Circle. And new Shape() { ... } with a class body compiles because it creates an anonymous subclass that supplies the missing methods, not an instance of Shape itself. An abstract class can still have fields and constructors, which run during subclass construction.

followups.q: Can an abstract class have no abstract methods?
followups.a: Yes. Marking it abstract still blocks direct instantiation, which suits a base class that should only exist through subclasses.

followups.q: What does getClass() return for new Shape() { ... }?
followups.a: A synthetic anonymous class that extends Shape, so it is not Shape.class.

questions.trap: Saying abstract types cannot be used at all. Abstract references are everywhere in polymorphism; only direct construction is forbidden.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 1.1 (Wissen). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-008.

questions.question: Can an abstract class declare a constructor, and when does it run?
questions.answer: Yes. The constructor is never reached through new on the abstract type, but it runs as part of the super() chain whenever a concrete subclass is instantiated. Its purpose is to initialise shared state and enforce invariants for every subclass, for example validating a required identifier before any subclass logic runs. If the abstract class declares only parameterised constructors, each subclass constructor must call one explicitly with super(args). A constructor should not call overridable methods, because the subclass fields are not yet initialised when it runs.

followups.q: What if the abstract class has no no-argument constructor?
followups.a: Every subclass constructor must call one of the declared constructors with super(...), otherwise compilation fails.

followups.q: Why is calling an overridable method from that constructor risky?
followups.a: The override can run before the subclass fields are initialised and observe default values.

questions.trap: Claiming abstract classes cannot have constructors because they cannot be instantiated. The constructor exists precisely for subclass construction.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 1.2 (Wissen). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-009.

questions.question: What happens when a class tries to extend two classes, and why does Java forbid it?
questions.answer: class A extends B, C is a syntax error. Java disallows multiple inheritance of implementation, meaning state and method bodies, because two superclasses could define the same field or method and the compiler would have no unambiguous way to choose: the diamond problem. Java does allow a class to implement many interfaces, which is multiple inheritance of type. Since Java 8, default methods can create a similar conflict, but the compiler forces the implementing class to resolve it explicitly, so the ambiguity never reaches runtime. To combine behaviours from several sources, use composition or interfaces with delegation.

followups.q: Can an interface extend several interfaces?
followups.a: Yes. Interface inheritance is allowed because it contributes a contract, and default-method conflicts are resolved by the implementer.

followups.q: How do you reuse behaviour from two classes then?
followups.a: Hold both as fields and delegate, or extract the shared behaviour into interfaces with default methods.

questions.trap: Stopping at 'compile error'. The interviewer wants the reason, ambiguous state and method resolution, and what to do instead.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 1.4 (Wissen). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-039, JH-S01-061.

questions.question: Why can an abstract method not be static, private or final?
questions.answer: abstract means a subclass must supply the body, so any modifier that prevents overriding contradicts it. final forbids overriding outright. private methods are invisible to subclasses, so they can never be overridden. static methods belong to the class and are bound at compile time, so a subclass can only hide them, not override them. The compiler therefore rejects each combination. The unifying rule is that an abstract method must be overridable, which requires it to be non-private, non-static and non-final so that polymorphic dispatch can select the subclass body.

followups.q: Can an interface method be private?
followups.a: Yes from Java 9, but it then needs a body and is only a helper inside the interface, not an overridable contract.

followups.q: Can an abstract class have a static method?
followups.a: Yes, provided the static method itself is not abstract; it simply is not polymorphic.

questions.trap: Giving three memorised reasons without the unifying idea that all three prevent a subclass from supplying the body.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 1.6 (Wissen). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-007, JH-S01-008.

questions.question: How do you achieve encapsulation in Java?
questions.answer: Encapsulation hides internal state behind a controlled interface so invariants cannot be broken from outside. Declare fields private, expose behaviour instead of raw data, for example account.withdraw(amount) rather than setBalance, and validate inside the methods that change state. Return defensive copies or unmodifiable views of mutable internals so callers cannot mutate them through a getter. Keep implementation types package-private or unexported from a module. Getters and setters alone are not encapsulation if they hand the internals out unchanged or accept any value.

followups.q: Is a class with private fields and a public getter and setter for each automatically encapsulated?
followups.a: No. If setters accept anything and getters return mutable internals, the invariants remain unprotected.

followups.q: How do records relate to encapsulation?
followups.a: A record is a shallowly immutable carrier; mutable components still need defensive copies in the compact constructor and accessors.

questions.trap: Defining encapsulation as 'private fields plus getters and setters'.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 1.7 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron)). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-005, JH-S01-011.

questions.question: Compare getters and setters, a singleton and an initializer block as ways to give a class its data, and state the order in which initialisation runs.
questions.answer: They solve different problems. Getters and setters give controlled per-object access to state and are the default choice. A singleton gives the whole application one shared instance, for configuration or a cache; an enum or a container-managed bean is safer than hand-written double-checked locking. An initializer block holds setup code shared by several constructors, or computes a final field that needs logic. At creation time the order is: static initializers once at class loading, then, for each object, the superclass constructor, then instance initializer blocks and field initializers, then the rest of this constructor body.

followups.q: Does the instance initializer run before or after super()?
followups.a: After the superclass constructor completes and before the remainder of this class's constructor body.

followups.q: Why prefer an enum or Spring bean over a hand-rolled singleton?
followups.a: Both avoid subtle double-checked locking, serialization and reflection pitfalls.

questions.trap: Treating the three as interchangeable alternatives instead of tools for different scopes: per object, per application and per construction.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 1.9 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron)). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-010.

questions.question: What is the difference between the transient keyword and JPA's @Transient annotation?
questions.answer: They share a name but act in different layers. The transient keyword excludes a field from Java's built-in serialization, so after deserialization it holds its default value. The @Transient annotation from jakarta.persistence tells the JPA provider not to map the field or property to a database column, which suits derived values such as a computed full name. The Java keyword also makes JPA skip the field, but the annotation is the explicit mapping-level choice and, unlike the keyword, has no effect on Java serialization. A cache field often needs both treatments. Neither is a JSON contract; for JSON use a library annotation such as @JsonIgnore.

followups.q: What value does a transient int field hold after deserialization?
followups.a: Its default, 0, unless readObject or readResolve restores it.

followups.q: How do you exclude a field from JSON output?
followups.a: With a JSON-library annotation such as Jackson's @JsonIgnore; neither transient nor @Transient is a JSON rule.

questions.trap: Assuming the JPA annotation stops Java serialization, or that the keyword is the only way to skip persistence.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 1.10 (company not recorded). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-048, JH-S07-053.

questions.question: What is the difference between an unchecked exception and an Error?
questions.answer: Both are unchecked, so the compiler does not force handling, and both descend from Throwable. An unchecked exception, meaning RuntimeException and its subclasses such as NullPointerException or IllegalArgumentException, signals a programming or contract violation that code can usually fix or handle at a sensible boundary, for example a controller advice that maps it to an HTTP response. An Error such as OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError or LinkageError signals a JVM or environment failure that the application generally cannot recover from, so it should not be caught and swallowed. Catch RuntimeException deliberately where you can act on it, and let Errors propagate to be handled operationally.

followups.q: Is it ever reasonable to catch an Error?
followups.a: Rarely: at a top-level boundary to log and fail the request or terminate cleanly. Continuing normal work after OutOfMemoryError is unsafe.

followups.q: How does a checked exception differ?
followups.a: It extends Exception but not RuntimeException, and the compiler requires a catch or a throws clause.

questions.trap: Saying Errors are checked, or that the two are the same because both are unchecked.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 1.13 (Impetus). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-004, JH-S01-029.
